title: Underused Value Angle: Science Class is Beautiful
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that teachers over-rely on utility ("when will I ever use this") to justify content and under-use a more powerful angle: beauty and meaning for their own sake. He illustrates the point with a long Rebecca Solnit passage about human skull development, showing how a writer with no scientific background used scientific knowledge to reach a level of insight and beauty otherwise unavailable to her. The example is meant to reframe science class specifically, and academic content generally, as valuable not just for future professional payoff but because it lets students experience delight, pattern, and meaning. Stuart closes by putting the responsibility for surfacing that beauty squarely on teachers, since no one else in a student's life is positioned to do it.
points: Names a specific, underused motivational lever - beauty/meaning rather than utility - within his "Rainbow of Why" framework for making content matter to students.
Uses a non-scientist writer's (Rebecca Solnit's) prose about human skull development to show how scientific knowledge enables a level of insight unreachable without it.
Reframes science's value away from future-career payoff (medicine, engineering) and toward the immediate experience of beauty and delight available to any student now.
Places responsibility for surfacing content's beauty on the teacher, arguing no one else in a student's world is positioned to do that work.
quotes: I think that in school we're way too quick to tell students "when they'll ever use this" (that's utility on the graphic above) and we're way too slow to paint a picture of how what we learn in school isn't just stuff to be used but is stuff that lets us experience pleasure and meaning and beauty.

Human infants are born with craniums made up of four plates that have not yet knit together into a solid dome so that their heads can compress to fit through the birth canal, so that the brain within can then expand.

Open enough to grow and closed enough to hold together is what a life must also be. We collage ourselves into being, finding the pieces of a worldview and people to love and reasons to live and then integrate them into a whole, a life consistent with its beliefs and desires, at least if we're lucky.
Learning things in science is not just valuable for future scientists. It's not just a thing that'll pay off for folks going into medicine or engineering.

Science is valuable for our students and worthy of their time because it enables them to experience beauty and meaning and purpose and delight that apart from science they'd not quite ever get to experience.
And the thing we teachers have to accept, of course, is that no one else is more responsible for helping our students to see this than we are.
